newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault, France eager to turn page on Vilvoorde.
newsitem.headline: Renault, France eager to turn page on Vilvoorde.

text.p: French political leaders rebuked carmaker Renault SA on Monday for going ahead with plans to close a factory in Belgium but seemed eager to turn the page on the embarrassing affair.

The Vilvoorde saga has been a difficult test for the new Socialist-led government, which is trying to fulfill campaign promises to protect jobs but is reluctant to block a restructuring of France's ailing car industry.
An aide to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who demonstrated in Brussels in March to protest the shutdown, explained on Monday that the affair was "too far gone to allow for backtracking".

Renault, which lost 5.25 billion francs last year, announced on Saturday that its board voted to proceed with the shutdown after an independent consultant agreed that reducing workweeks -- the Socialists' big theme -- was not an alternative solution.

"Cutting working hours on all the sites without a profound reorganisation would not resolve the economic problems," said Danielle Kaisergruber's report, which was commissioned this month days after the election of a Socialist government.
"The industry trend is toward the development of bigger factories running on three shifts," Kaisergruber said.
Her report confirmed Renault's assessment that its sites were too small and scattered relative to its competitors in Europe and that the assembly operation needed to be streamlined.
Vilvoorde was vulnerable because it was among the smallest and costliest plants to run and it was not the mother plant for any new model.
Renault managers were expected to meet union representatives on Monday to discuss the closure, amid pressures to work out a generous settlement for the 2,900 workers still at the factory.
"Even if it's not my jurisdiction, I want the job-cutting programme to be a real programme to enable each worker to find another job," Labour Minister Martine Aubry said on Monday.
"We're demanding that the government keep up the pressure on Renault for a more generous job-reduction plan to prevent outright layoffs," a Socialist Party spokesman said.
"We have to draw a lesson from what happened and make use of reduced working hours, notably in the car sector and especially at Renault," the spokesman said.
The state is Renault's biggest shareholder with 46 percent.
"The government's drawing the line at Belgium. They're saying, 'Don't do it in France,'" a share analyst said.
Both PSA Peugeot Citroen and Renault plan close to 3,000 job cuts each in France this year, a slight acceleration from recent years, but no outright layoffs.
Both resist pressure to shorten workweeks, and analysts agree such a move would only increase the French industry's already excessive costs.
The Peugeot group's chairman Jacques Calvet last week said his company would not consider reducing workweeks to 35 from 39 hours without a corresponding cut in wages.
Cutting workweeks alone "won't create more jobs but more unemployment," Calvet told the annual general meeting.
Aides to Jospin signalled that the government was cautious in taking on the car industry, France's biggest employer accounting for more than 700,000 direct and indirect jobs.

One adviser said reducing hours works best in industries functioning at or close to full capacity, while the auto industry is struggling to cope with huge overcapacity that has fuelled a price war in Europe.
Renault estimates its share of the overcapacity in Europe at 200,000 cars annually -- roughly one plant's turnout.
Its stock fell 4.37 percent to 148.70 francs on Monday after investors took profits on its 5.5 percent gain on Thursday and Friday on expectations the shutdown would be confirmed.
